Before the seminar

The lecture proved one result, the adjustment theorem, which you prove again with the slides closed (exercise 3). It stated the optimal threshold theorem and no free lunch and left proofs to you (exercises 1 and 4), and it stated the confounding gap without deriving it (exercise 2). Do all four on paper before the seminar; the seminar’s problems are variations on exercises 1 to 3. You may use, without proof, two facts from ST102: the tower property, \(\mathbb E[W] = \mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[W \mid X]\big]\), and that if \(V\) is independent of \(X\), then \(\mathbb E[k(X, V) \mid X = x] = \mathbb E[k(x, V)]\) for any function \(k\) (freeze \(X\) at \(x\); the distribution of \(V\) does not move).

WarningHints

Each exercise has hints, collapsed below it. Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few minutes, and open them in order. Exercise 3’s proof is on the lecture slides. Solutions to exercises 1, 2 and 4 are shown in the seminar if you ask.

Exercise 1 (optimal threshold theorem). Let \(p(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)\). A false positive (predict \(1\), truth \(0\)) costs \(c_{FP} \ge 0\), a false negative (predict \(0\), truth \(1\)) costs \(c_{FN} \ge 0\), not both are \(0\), and a correct prediction costs nothing. A rule \(\delta\) assigns a prediction \(\delta(x) \in \{0, 1\}\) to every \(x\).

  1. At a fixed \(x\), write the expected cost of predicting \(1\) and the expected cost of predicting \(0\).

  2. Show that predicting \(1\) has the smaller expected cost exactly when \(p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\). What happens at \(p(x) = c^\star\)?

  3. Let \(\delta^\star\) be the rule from (b). Show that \(\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta^\star(X), Y)\big] \le \mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y)\big]\) for every rule \(\delta\).

  4. With equal costs, what is \(c^\star\), and what is the probability of a wrong label at \(x\) under \(\delta^\star\)?

NoteHint 1

Given \(X = x\), \(Y\) is \(1\) with probability \(p(x)\). If you predict \(1\), when is that a mistake, and what does the mistake cost?

NoteHint 2
  1. Compare the two expected costs and solve the inequality for \(p(x)\). “Not both \(0\)” is what lets you divide.
NoteHint 3
  1. Condition on \(X\) first (the tower property), as in week 2’s exercise 1. What do you know about the inner expectation, at every \(x\)?
TipReveal solution

  1. Predicting \(1\) is a mistake when \(Y = 0\), which has probability \(1 - p(x)\), and then costs \(c_{FP}\); predicting \(0\) is a mistake when \(Y = 1\), probability \(p(x)\), cost \(c_{FN}\): \[ \mathbb E[\text{cost} \mid \text{predict } 1,\ X = x] = c_{FP}\,(1 - p(x)), \qquad \mathbb E[\text{cost} \mid \text{predict } 0,\ X = x] = c_{FN}\, p(x). \]

  2. Predicting \(1\) is cheaper when \[ c_{FN}\,p > c_{FP}\,(1 - p) \iff p\,(c_{FP} + c_{FN}) > c_{FP} \iff p > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}, \] dividing by \(c_{FP} + c_{FN} > 0\). At \(p(x) = c^\star\) the two expected costs are equal, so either prediction is optimal.

  3. For any rule \(\delta\), by the tower property, \[ \mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y)\big] = \mathbb E_X\Big[\,\mathbb E\big[\text{cost}(\delta(X), Y) \mid X\big]\Big]. \] At \(X = x\) the inner expectation is the expected cost of the prediction \(\delta(x)\) from (a), and by (b) it is at least the expected cost of \(\delta^\star(x)\). An inequality that holds at every \(x\) survives averaging over \(X\). \(\blacksquare\) This is week 2’s step: minimize the expected loss at each \(x\), then average.

  4. \(c^\star = \tfrac12\): predict the more probable class, the Bayes classifier. The probability of a wrong label at \(x\) is \(1 - p(x)\) if you predict \(1\) and \(p(x)\) if you predict \(0\), so under \(\delta^\star\) it is \(\min(p(x), 1 - p(x))\). Equal costs make the expected cost a multiple of the probability of error, so by (c) no rule has a smaller overall probability of error.

Common errors: the ratio upside down, \(c_{FN}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\) (check an extreme: if a miss were infinitely costly the threshold must go to \(0\), and only \(c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\) does that); choosing one threshold to minimize the overall cost directly, without the argument at each \(x\); reading the theorem as a statement about \(\hat p\). It is about the true \(p(x)\); with \(\hat p\) in its place the rule is a plug-in rule, only as good as the estimate.

Exercise 2 (confounding gap). The lecture’s DAG made linear. \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) are independent, \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) have mean \(0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(T) > 0\), and \[ T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T, \qquad Y = \tau T + \gamma Z + \varepsilon_Y. \]

  1. Under \(do(T = t)\), which variables keep their values? Show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \tau t + \gamma\, \mathbb E Z\), so that moving \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\) changes the mean of \(Y\) by \(\tau\).

  2. As observed, show that \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t] = \tau t + \gamma\, \mathbb E[Z \mid T = t]\), and hence \[ \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Y \mid T = 0] = \tau + \gamma\,\big(\mathbb E[Z \mid T = 1] - \mathbb E[Z \mid T = 0]\big). \] Where did you use independence?

  3. Show that the population slope of the least-squares line of \(Y\) on \(T\) alone, \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(T)\), is \(\tau + \gamma\,\delta\) with \(\delta = \mathrm{Cov}(Z, T)/\mathrm{Var}(T)\). Which quantity in week 2’s omitted-variable bias plays the role of \(\delta\)?

  4. When is the gap zero?

NoteHint 1
  1. Delete \(T\)’s equation and set \(T = t\). Is \(Z\) upstream or downstream of \(T\)?
NoteHint 2
  1. Take \(\mathbb E[\,\cdot \mid T = t]\) of \(Y\)’s equation term by term. \(T\) is a function of \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon_T\); what does that say about \(\varepsilon_Y\) and \(T\)?
NoteHint 3
  1. Expand \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)\) using \(Y\)’s equation. \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y) = 0\) for the reason you found in (b).
TipReveal solution

  1. \(Z\) is upstream of \(T\) and the noises are their own, so \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) keep their values: \(Y = \tau t + \gamma Z + \varepsilon_Y\), and \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \tau t + \gamma\,\mathbb E Z + 0\). The difference between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 0\) is \(\tau\), the coefficient on \(T\) in \(Y\)’s own equation.

  2. \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t] = \tau t + \gamma\,\mathbb E[Z \mid T = t] + \mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t]\). \(T = \alpha Z + \varepsilon_T\) is a function of \((Z, \varepsilon_T)\), and \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \((Z, \varepsilon_T)\), so \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \(T\) and \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t] = \mathbb E\,\varepsilon_Y = 0\). That is where independence is used. Subtracting the expressions at \(t = 1\) and \(t = 0\) gives the gap. \(\blacksquare\)

  3. \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = \tau\,\mathrm{Var}(T) + \gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) + \mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y)\), and the last term is \(0\). Dividing by \(\mathrm{Var}(T)\) gives \(\tau + \gamma\,\delta\). Here \(\delta\), the population slope of \(Z\) on \(T\), plays the role of \(\hat\delta\) (the slope of the omitted \(\mathbf x_2\) on the kept \(\mathbf x_1\)), \(\tau\) plays \(\beta_1\) and \(\gamma\) plays \(\beta_2\): omitted-variable bias, read causally. With these equations \(\delta = \alpha\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)/(\alpha^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Z) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_T))\).

  4. When \(\gamma = 0\) (\(Z\) does not affect \(Y\)), or when the mean of \(Z\) does not move with \(T\); for example \(\alpha = 0\), when \(T\) does not depend on \(Z\) at all, which is what randomizing \(T\) arranges. (The gap in (b) compares two conditional means; the slope in (c) is a least-squares slope. They agree, gap \(= \gamma\delta\), when \(\mathbb E[Z \mid T]\) is linear in \(T\), as it is when everything is normal.)

Common errors: letting \(Z\) change under the intervention; writing \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t] = 0\) without saying why (it needs the independence, which an unobserved common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\) would break); writing the bias as \(\gamma\alpha\) instead of \(\gamma\delta\).

Exercise 3 (adjustment theorem). The lecture proved this one. Close the slides and prove it again. Structural model: \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent, \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\), \(Y = g(T, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\); under \(do(T = t)\) the equation for \(T\) is deleted, \(T\) is set to \(t\), and everything else keeps its equation and its noise. Show that, wherever \(P(T = t \mid Z) > 0\), \[ \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\,\Big], \] and say where each assumption is used: the independence of the noises, \(Z\) not being a consequence of \(T\), and \(P(T = t \mid Z) > 0\).

NoteHint 1

Start from the intervened world. What is \(Y\) under \(do(T = t)\), and which variables keep their values? Give the average over the noise with \(Z\) frozen a name: \(m_t(z) = \mathbb E\big[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\big]\).

NoteHint 2

Use the second ST102 fact, with \(V = \varepsilon_Y\) and \(Z\) in the role of \(X\), to show \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big]\).

NoteHint 3

Now the observed world: on \(\{T = t, Z = z\}\), \(Y = g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\). Why is \(\varepsilon_Y\) independent of \((T, Z)\), and what does that give for \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\)?

NoteHint 4

Why is the distribution of \(Z\) the same in the observed and the intervened worlds?

TipReveal solution

The lecture’s lines. Hint 1: under \(do(T = t)\), \(Y = g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\), with \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) unchanged (\(Z\) is upstream of \(T\)). Hint 2: \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \(Z\), so \(\mathbb E[g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y) \mid Z = z] = m_t(z)\), and by the tower property \[ \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E\big[g(t, Z, \varepsilon_Y)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big]. \] Hint 3: \(T = h(Z, \varepsilon_T)\) is a function of \((Z, \varepsilon_T)\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \((Z, \varepsilon_T)\), so \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \((T, Z)\). Wherever \(P(T = t \mid Z = z) > 0\), the event \(\{T = t, Z = z\}\) can be conditioned on, and on it \(Y = g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y)\), so \[ \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = \mathbb E\big[g(t, z, \varepsilon_Y) \mid T = t, Z = z\big] = m_t(z). \] Hint 4: \(Z\) is upstream of \(T\), so the intervention does not change it, and its distribution is the same in the two worlds. Averaging the last display over it, \[ \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E_Z\big[m_t(Z)\big] = \mathbb E_Z\Big[\,\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z]\,\Big]. \qquad \blacksquare \] Where each assumption is used: the independence of the noises in the observed-world step (a common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\) left out of \(Z\) would sit in both \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\), making them dependent); \(Z\) not a consequence of \(T\) in the intervened-world step (a \(Z\) downstream of \(T\) would change when \(T\) is set, and its distribution would differ between the worlds); \(P(T = t \mid Z) > 0\) so that the conditional mean exists (for a continuous \(T\), read it as the conditional density being positive). If \(Z\) is empty, \(T = h(\varepsilon_T)\) is independent of \(\varepsilon_Y\) and the same lines give \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t]\): randomization.

Common errors: letting \(Z\) respond to the intervention; asserting \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = m_t(z)\) without the independence of \(\varepsilon_Y\) from \((T, Z)\); reading the theorem as “regress \(Y\) on \(T\) and \(Z\) and take the coefficient”, which is one way to estimate the inside when the conditional mean is linear, not what the theorem says.

Exercise 4 (no free lunch on a finite domain). A finite set \(\mathcal X\) has \(N\) points. A labeling is a function \(f: \mathcal X \to \{0, 1\}\). A method sees the labels on a fixed training set \(S \subset \mathcal X\) of \(m < N\) points and returns a classifier \(\hat h\), which may be any function of those \(m\) labels. Its error on the points it has not seen is \[ \mathrm{err}(\hat h, f) = \frac{1}{N - m} \sum_{x \notin S} \mathbb 1\big[\hat h(x) \ne f(x)\big]. \]

  1. Draw \(f\) uniformly at random from all \(2^N\) labelings. Show that \(\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{err}(\hat h, f)\big] = \tfrac12\) for every method.

  2. Two methods, \(A\) and \(B\). Suppose \(A\)’s error on the unseen points is smaller than \(B\)’s for some labeling. Show that \(B\)’s is smaller than \(A\)’s for another labeling.

  3. What would have to be true of the world for some method to do better than \(\tfrac12\) on average?

NoteHint 1

Uniform over all \(2^N\) labelings means that the \(N\) labels \(f(x)\) are independent fair coin flips.

NoteHint 2

Fix \(x \notin S\). \(\hat h(x)\) depends only on the labels on \(S\), and \(f(x)\) is independent of them. Condition on the labels on \(S\): what is \(P\big(\hat h(x) \ne f(x)\big)\)?

NoteHint 3
  1. Average \(\mathrm{err}(\hat h_A, f) - \mathrm{err}(\hat h_B, f)\) over all \(2^N\) labelings.
TipReveal solution

  1. Under the uniform distribution the \(N\) labels are independent fair coin flips. Fix \(x \notin S\). Given the labels on \(S\), \(\hat h(x)\) is a fixed number, \(0\) or \(1\), and \(f(x)\) is still a fair coin flip, independent of those labels, so \(P(\hat h(x) \ne f(x) \mid \text{labels on } S) = \tfrac12\), and so \(P(\hat h(x) \ne f(x)) = \tfrac12\). Averaging over the \(N - m\) unseen points, \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{err}(\hat h, f)] = \tfrac12\). \(\blacksquare\)

  2. By (a), the average of \(\mathrm{err}(\hat h_A, f) - \mathrm{err}(\hat h_B, f)\) over all labelings is \(\tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0\). A difference that averages to zero and is negative for one labeling must be positive for another.

  3. The labelings must not all be equally likely: the labels on \(S\) have to carry information about the labels off \(S\), for example because nearby points tend to share a label, or because \(f\) is a threshold of a linear score. Every method bets on some such structure (the nearest-neighbor method bets on the first, logistic regression on the second), and the bet pays off only on the labelings that have it. Choosing a method is choosing the bet.

Common errors: forgetting that the claim is about the points the method has not seen (on \(S\) itself a method can be perfect); reading it as “all methods are equally good on the problems we meet”, which it does not say, because those problems are not uniformly random labelings.

Problems

Problem 1 (costs 5 and 1). A conservation survey classifies penguins from a photograph. Labeling a Chinstrap as an Adelie (a miss) wastes a return visit, cost 5; labeling an Adelie as a Chinstrap (a false alarm) wastes a phone call, cost 1. Write \(p(x) = P(\text{Chinstrap} \mid x)\).

  1. Find the threshold on \(p(x)\) above which predicting Chinstrap has the smaller expected cost. What happens at the threshold itself?

  2. A fitted model gives \(\hat p = 0.25\) for one bird. What does the rule predict, and what would have to be true of \(\hat p\) for that prediction to be the best one at that \(x\)?

  3. The survey hands the same \(\hat p\) to two field teams. For team A a miss costs 5 and a false alarm 1; for team B both cost 1. For which values of \(\hat p\) do the two teams make different calls?

  4. Say in one sentence what the survey decided when it chose 5 and 1.

NoteHint 1
  1. Which kind of mistake is the false positive here, and which the false negative? Then exercise 1(b).
NoteHint 2
  1. Each team has its own threshold. Between the two thresholds, what does each team predict?
TipReveal answer

  1. Predicting Chinstrap is a false alarm when the bird is an Adelie: \(c_{FP} = 1\), \(c_{FN} = 5\). Expected costs \(1 \cdot (1 - p)\) and \(5p\), so Chinstrap is cheaper when \(p > 1/6 \approx 0.167\). At \(p = 1/6\) the two costs are equal and either prediction is optimal.

  2. \(\hat p = 0.25 > 1/6\), so the rule says Chinstrap. That is the best decision at \(x\) only if \(\hat p\) is the true \(p(x)\). With an estimate in its place it is a plug-in rule: if the model is badly calibrated there (say the true \(p(x)\) is \(0.1\)) the call is wrong.

  3. Team A’s threshold is \(1/6\), team B’s is \(1/2\). For \(1/6 < \hat p < 1/2\), A calls Chinstrap and B calls Adelie; at the two end points one team is indifferent. Same model, same bird, different decisions: the difference comes from the costs alone.

  4. That five false alarms are worth one miss: a statement about the survey’s resources, not about penguins.

Common errors: swapping the costs (threshold \(5/6\)); “the model predicts Chinstrap”, when the model gives a probability and the rule makes the call.

Problem 2 (the lecture’s DAG, with numbers). Let \(Z\) have mean \(0\) and variance \(1\); let \(T = Z + \varepsilon_T\) and \(Y = T + 2Z + \varepsilon_Y\), where \(\varepsilon_T\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\) have mean \(0\) and variance \(1\), and \(Z\), \(\varepsilon_T\), \(\varepsilon_Y\) are independent.

  1. What is the effect on \(\mathbb E[Y]\) of raising \(t\) by one under \(do(T = t)\)?

  2. Compute \(\mathrm{Var}(T)\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y)\) and the population slope of the regression of \(Y\) on \(T\) alone. Write it as “effect plus gap” and identify the gap.

  3. Compute \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\), average it over \(Z\), and check that you recover (a). Where did you use that the noises are independent?

  4. A world where the causation runs the other way: \(Y = \varepsilon_Y\) with variance \(4\), and \(T = 0.4\,Y + \varepsilon_T\), with \(\varepsilon_T\) of variance \(0.16\), independent of \(Y\). Find the population slope of \(Y\) on \(T\) and the effect of raising \(t\) by one.

NoteHint 1
  1. and (b) are exercise 2 with \(\alpha = \tau = 1\) and \(\gamma = 2\). For the covariance, \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) = \mathrm{Var}(Z)\) here.
NoteHint 2
  1. Take \(\mathbb E[\,\cdot \mid T = t, Z = z]\) of \(Y\)’s equation. (d) \(\mathrm{Var}(T) = 0.4^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Y) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_T)\).
TipReveal answer

  1. Under \(do(T = t)\), \(Y = t + 2Z + \varepsilon_Y\), so \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] = t\) and raising \(t\) by one raises it by \(1\).

  2. \(\mathrm{Var}(T) = 1 + 1 = 2\). \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = \mathrm{Var}(T) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) + \mathrm{Cov}(T, \varepsilon_Y) = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4\). Slope \(4/2 = 2 = 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac12\): the effect \(\tau = 1\) plus the gap \(\gamma\delta = 2 \cdot \tfrac12\), with \(\delta = \mathrm{Cov}(Z, T)/\mathrm{Var}(T) = \tfrac12\). The naive slope credits \(T\) with what \(Z\) contributes through selection, and here the gap is as large as the effect.

  3. \(\mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = t + 2z + \mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = t + 2z\), because \(\varepsilon_Y\) is independent of \((Z, \varepsilon_T)\) and so of \((T, Z)\). Averaging over \(Z\): \(\mathbb E_Z[t + 2Z] = t\), which is (a). The independence is what made \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_Y \mid T = t, Z = z]\) zero.

  4. \(\mathrm{Var}(T) = 0.16 \cdot 4 + 0.16 = 0.8\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Y) = 0.4 \cdot 4 = 1.6\), slope \(2\). The effect is \(0\): \(Y\)’s equation has no \(T\) in it, and setting \(T\) changes nothing upstream. The same population slope as (b), and as a world with \(Y = 2T + \varepsilon\): the regression alone cannot tell the three apart.

Common errors: in (a), letting \(Z\) change when \(T\) is set; in (b), \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, Z) = 0\); in (d), “the slope is 2, so the effect is 2”.

Optional, can be done at home

Problem 3 (what no free lunch says). Which of these claims does exercise 4 support? (a) “Nearest neighbors is a better method than linear regression.” (b) “On the gapminder data, nearest neighbors beat the line.” (c) “A method that makes no assumptions would beat all the others.”

NoteHint 1

For each claim: is it about one distribution, every distribution, or the average over all labelings?

TipReveal answer
  1. Not supported as stated: “better” needs a distribution, and on some labelings each method does better than the other. (b) Fine, as a statement about one dataset and one split, with a standard error (week 1). (c) The opposite: on a finite domain a method that makes no assumption about how the labels hang together has error \(\tfrac12\) on the unseen points, like every other method on average; a method does better only where its assumption holds. Choosing a method is the assumption.

Common errors: reading no free lunch as “all methods are equally good” on the problems we actually meet.

Problem 4 (a model that predicts well). A hospital fits a model that predicts which patients will be readmitted within 30 days, and it predicts well on held-out patients. Management proposes to reduce readmissions by acting on the model’s strongest predictor. Draw the DAGs of three worlds consistent with that held-out score, say in which of them the plan works, and say what the score told you about which world you are in.

NoteHint 1

The lecture’s three worlds: the predictor causes readmission, a common cause drives both, or readmission risk drives the predictor.

TipReveal answer

A: the predictor causes readmission (for example, discharge before a test result is back); acting on it can work. B: a common cause such as severity drives both; acting on the predictor changes nothing. C: readmission risk drives the predictor (for example, patients at high risk are put on extra monitoring, and the monitoring is the predictor); acting on it changes nothing, and stopping the monitoring could do harm. The held-out score is the same in all three, so it told you nothing about which world you are in. Deciding needs knowledge of the mechanism, or an experiment.

Common errors: “the model is accurate, so the predictor is a cause”; drawing world C with the arrow the wrong way round.

Coding

1. Penguins: a probability and a threshold

Adelie against Chinstrap, from the bill. Keep the two species and the birds with complete measurements.

pg <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>   # modeldata also has a penguins; be explicit
  filter(species != "Gentoo") |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm) |>
  mutate(chinstrap = as.numeric(species == "Chinstrap"))
ggplot(pg, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.7)

Step 1. How many birds, and what proportion are Chinstraps? What accuracy would a classifier that always predicts the more common species achieve?

# nrow(pg); mean(pg$____)
# max(____, 1 - ____)
# ...
TipReveal solution 
nrow(pg)
[1] 219
mean(pg$chinstrap)
[1] 0.3105023
max(mean(pg$chinstrap), 1 - mean(pg$chinstrap))
[1] 0.6894977

Step 2. Fit the logistic regression of chinstrap on the two bill measurements with glm(..., family = binomial). Look at tidy(), then at tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE).

# fit_bill <- glm(____ ~ ____ + ____, family = binomial, data = pg)
# tidy(fit_bill)
# tidy(fit_bill, exponentiate = TRUE)
# ...
TipReveal solution 
fit_bill <- glm(chinstrap ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
tidy(fit_bill)
# A tibble: 3 x 5
  term           estimate std.error statistic p.value
  <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 (Intercept)      -24.1     13.5       -1.78 0.0744 
2 bill_length_mm     2.20     0.687      3.20 0.00136
3 bill_depth_mm     -3.98     1.49      -2.67 0.00759
tidy(fit_bill, exponentiate = TRUE)
# A tibble: 3 x 5
  term           estimate std.error statistic p.value
  <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 (Intercept)    3.43e-11    13.5       -1.78 0.0744 
2 bill_length_mm 9.03e+ 0     0.687      3.20 0.00136
3 bill_depth_mm  1.87e- 2     1.49      -2.67 0.00759

Checkpoint (run it; if it stops, fix step 2 before going on):

stopifnot(inherits(fit_bill, "glm"), length(coef(fit_bill)) == 3,
          all(fitted(fit_bill) >= 0 & fitted(fit_bill) <= 1))

You may have seen a warning that fitted probabilities are numerically 0 or 1: the two species are nearly separable on these two measurements (step 3 counts the errors). This is the lecture’s “Challenges” slide in real life; next week says what it does to the fitting.

Question 1. Read the exponentiated coefficient on bill_length_mm. What happens to the odds of Chinstrap when bill length increases by one millimeter and bill depth is held fixed? Is that the change in the probability? Is it what would happen to a bird whose bill grew by a millimeter?

TipReveal answer

The odds of Chinstrap are multiplied by about \(e^{2.20} \approx 9.0\) per millimeter, with bill depth held fixed. That is a multiplier on the odds \(p/(1 - p)\), not a change in \(p\): how much \(p\) moves depends on where it starts (near \(0\) or \(1\) a ninefold change in the odds moves \(p\) very little; near \(\tfrac12\) it moves it a lot). The standard error is large (\(0.69\) on the log-odds scale, so the interval for the multiplier runs from about \(2\) to about \(35\)), because the classes are nearly separable. And “holding depth fixed” is the lecture’s ceteris paribus: a comparison between birds in the fitted model, not what would happen to one bird if its bill grew. Nothing here is causal.

Step 3. The confusion matrix at threshold \(\tfrac12\), with table(). From it, compute the accuracy, the true positive rate and the false positive rate.

# p_hat <- fitted(fit_bill)
# tab <- table(truth = pg$chinstrap, predicted = as.numeric(p_hat > ____))
# tab
# accuracy <- (tab[1, 1] + tab[2, 2]) / sum(tab)
# tpr <- ____ ; fpr <- ____
# ...
TipReveal solution 
p_hat <- fitted(fit_bill)
tab <- table(truth = pg$chinstrap, predicted = as.numeric(p_hat > 0.5))
tab
     predicted
truth   0   1
    0 148   3
    1   3  65
accuracy <- (tab[1, 1] + tab[2, 2]) / sum(tab)
tpr <- tab[2, 2] / sum(tab[2, ])
fpr <- tab[1, 2] / sum(tab[1, ])
c(accuracy = accuracy, tpr = tpr, fpr = fpr)
  accuracy        tpr        fpr 
0.97260274 0.95588235 0.01986755

Checkpoint:

stopifnot(sum(tab) == nrow(pg), tpr >= 0, tpr <= 1, fpr >= 0, fpr <= 1)

Step 4. The bill model is nearly perfect, so it cannot show the trade-off. Fit a weaker model on flipper_length_mm alone, then compute the ROC curve yourself: for thresholds from 0 to 1, the true positive rate and the false positive rate. Plot one against the other. The loop is set up; you write the two rates.

fit_flipper <- glm(chinstrap ~ flipper_length_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
pg <- pg |> mutate(p_flipper = fitted(fit_flipper))
thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
roc_by_hand <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  # tibble(t = t,
  #        tpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 1) / sum(____),
  #        fpr = sum(____) / sum(____))
  # ...
})
# ggplot(roc_by_hand, aes(____, ____)) + geom_path() + coord_equal()
# ...
TipReveal solution 
fit_flipper <- glm(chinstrap ~ flipper_length_mm, family = binomial, data = pg)
pg <- pg |> mutate(p_flipper = fitted(fit_flipper))
thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
roc_by_hand <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  tibble(t = t,
         tpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 1) / sum(pg$chinstrap == 1),
         fpr = sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 0) / sum(pg$chinstrap == 0))
})
ggplot(roc_by_hand, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_equal()

Checkpoint:

stopifnot(nrow(roc_by_hand) == length(thresholds),
          all(roc_by_hand$tpr >= 0 & roc_by_hand$tpr <= 1),
          roc_by_hand$tpr[1] == 1, roc_by_hand$fpr[1] == 1)

Question 2. The area under your curve equals the probability that a randomly chosen Chinstrap gets a higher fitted probability than a randomly chosen Adelie, with a tie counting half. Why does accumulating one point per threshold produce that probability? Why are ties certain to occur with this model?

TipReveal answer

Moving the threshold down past one bird’s score adds that bird to the predicted Chinstraps: a Chinstrap raises the TPR by \(1/n_1\), an Adelie raises the FPR by \(1/n_0\). The area under the path therefore adds up, for each Adelie step to the right, the height of the curve there, which is the fraction of Chinstraps already passed, those scoring above that Adelie. Summing over Adelies and dividing by \(n_0\) gives the fraction of (Chinstrap, Adelie) pairs in which the Chinstrap scores higher; a tie is a diagonal step and contributes half. Ties are certain because flipper_length_mm is recorded in whole millimeters and \(\hat p\) is a monotone function of it, so birds with the same flipper length have the same score; about 4 percent of the Chinstrap and Adelie pairs tie. By hand:

p1 <- pg$p_flipper[pg$chinstrap == 1]
p0 <- pg$p_flipper[pg$chinstrap == 0]
mean(outer(p1, p0, ">") + 0.5 * outer(p1, p0, "=="))
[1] 0.7337846

Step 5. Costs. A miss costs 5, a false alarm 1. For each threshold compute the cost per bird on the 219 birds, \(5 \cdot (\text{misses}/n) + 1 \cdot (\text{false alarms}/n)\), find the threshold that minimizes it, and compare with problem 1’s threshold.

# costs <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
#   yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
#   tibble(t = t, cost = (5 * sum(____) + 1 * sum(____)) / nrow(pg))
# })
# ggplot(costs, aes(t, cost)) + geom_line()
# costs |> slice_min(cost, n = 3)
# ...
TipReveal solution 
costs <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) {
  yhat <- as.numeric(pg$p_flipper > t)
  tibble(t = t,
         cost = (5 * sum(yhat == 0 & pg$chinstrap == 1) + 1 * sum(yhat == 1 & pg$chinstrap == 0)) / nrow(pg))
})
ggplot(costs, aes(t, cost)) + geom_line()
costs |> slice_min(cost, n = 3)
# A tibble: 3 x 2
      t  cost
  <dbl> <dbl>
1  0.16 0.580
2  0.17 0.580
3  0.15 0.612
c(formula = 1 / (1 + 5))
  formula 
0.1666667

Checkpoint:

stopifnot(nrow(costs) == length(thresholds), all(costs$cost >= 0))

Question 3. The cost-minimizing threshold is well below \(\tfrac12\), and the classifier now raises many false alarms. Who decided that, and in what sense is this classifier “better” than the one at \(\tfrac12\)? Is the number you found the population optimum?

TipReveal answer

The survey did, by choosing costs 5 and 1; the model contributed only \(\hat p\). It is better in expected cost under those costs and worse in accuracy: “better” has no meaning until a loss is chosen. The formula gives the population optimum for the true \(p(x)\); the curve is an empirical cost on the birds the model was fitted to, with \(\hat p\) plugged in, and its minimum is flat (several thresholds near \(1/6\) tie). So the agreement is between an estimate and the formula, not a proof that the formula is right for new birds. That evaluating on the training rows flatters the model is the validation week’s subject.

2. Four worlds, and the adjustment theorem in code

Four simulated worlds in which \(Y\) is regressed on \(X\). In the lecture the target variable was called \(T\); here it is X, because T is TRUE in R. The function draws the noise once and keeps it, so that an intervention can be computed for the same units. World D is the lecture’s DAG with the confounder \(Z\) observed: \(Z \to X\), \(Z \to Y\), \(X \to Y\).

simulate_world <- function(world, n = 500) {
  e_u <- rnorm(n)
  e_x <- rnorm(n)
  e_y <- rnorm(n)
  if (world == "A") {           # X causes Y
    X <- e_x
    Y <- 2 * X + e_y
    Z <- NA
  } else if (world == "B") {    # U causes both; U is not observed
    U <- e_u
    X <- U + 0.5 * e_x
    Y <- 2.5 * U + e_y
    Z <- NA
  } else if (world == "C") {    # Y causes X
    Y <- 2 * e_y
    X <- 0.4 * Y + 0.4 * e_x
    Z <- NA
  } else {                      # D: Z causes both, and X causes Y; Z is observed
    Z <- e_u
    X <- 5 - 2 * Z + e_x
    Y <- 4 + 2 * Z - 3 * X + e_y
  }
  tibble(world = world, X = X, Y = Y, Z = Z, e_u = e_u, e_x = e_x, e_y = e_y)
}
worlds <- bind_rows(simulate_world("A"), simulate_world("B"), simulate_world("C"), simulate_world("D"))

Step 1. In each world, fit lm(Y ~ X) and report the slope.

# worlds |>
#   group_by(world) |>
#   summarise(slope = coef(lm(____))[2])
# ...
TipReveal solution 
worlds |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2])
# A tibble: 4 x 2
  world slope
  <chr> <dbl>
1 A      1.99
2 B      2.03
3 C      2.01
4 D     -3.82

Question 4. Before you intervene: for each world, write down what you expect to happen to \(Y\) when \(X\) is set to \(X + 1\) for every unit with the same noise, and the average change. Use each world’s equations, and exercise 2 for world D.

TipReveal answer

A: \(Y\) rises by exactly \(2\) for every unit (its equation has \(2X\)). B: nothing; \(Y\) depends on \(U\) and its own noise only. C: nothing; \(Y\) is upstream of \(X\). D: \(Y\) falls by exactly \(3\) for every unit, the coefficient on \(X\) in \(Y\)’s equation, while the slope in step 1 is about \(-3.8\): \(\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(X) = (2 \cdot (-2) - 3 \cdot 5)/5 = -19/5\), the effect \(-3\) plus the confounding gap \(2 \cdot (-2/5)\).

Step 2. Now intervene: set \(X\) to \(X + 1\) for every unit and recompute \(Y\) with the same noise, following each world’s equations. Write the four Y_do lines and compute the average change in \(Y\) in each world.

intervene <- function(d) {
  d |> mutate(
    X_do = X + 1,
    # Y_do = case_when(
    #   world == "A" ~ ____,
    #   world == "B" ~ ____,
    #   world == "C" ~ ____,
    #   world == "D" ~ ____
    # )
    # ...
  )
}
worlds_do <- intervene(worlds)
worlds_do |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2],
            effect_of_intervention = mean(Y_do - Y))
TipReveal solution 
intervene <- function(d) {
  d |> mutate(
    X_do = X + 1,
    Y_do = case_when(
      world == "A" ~ 2 * X_do + e_y,
      world == "B" ~ 2.5 * e_u + e_y,
      world == "C" ~ Y,
      world == "D" ~ 4 + 2 * Z - 3 * X_do + e_y
    )
  )
}
worlds_do <- intervene(worlds)
worlds_do |>
  group_by(world) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2],
            effect_of_intervention = mean(Y_do - Y))
# A tibble: 4 x 3
  world slope effect_of_intervention
  <chr> <dbl>                  <dbl>
1 A      1.99                      2
2 B      2.03                      0
3 C      2.01                      0
4 D     -3.82                     -3

Checkpoint:

stopifnot(all(c("X_do", "Y_do") %in% names(worlds_do)),
          abs(mean(worlds_do$Y_do[worlds_do$world == "C"] - worlds_do$Y[worlds_do$world == "C"])) < 1e-8)

The average change is the average treatment effect of the intervention, \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(X = x + 1)] - \mathbb E[Y \mid do(X = x)]\), computed on these units: exactly \(2\), \(0\), \(0\) and \(-3\), because the noise was reused.

Step 3. World D, the adjustment theorem in code. Regress Y on X and Z and read off the coefficient on X. Then do what the theorem says: fit \(\hat m(x, z)\) for \(\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x, Z = z]\) (the same regression), evaluate it at every unit’s \(Z\) with \(X\) set to \(X + 1\) and to \(X\), and average the difference.

d <- worlds |> filter(world == "D")
# fit_d <- lm(Y ~ ____ + ____, data = d)
# tidy(fit_d)
# mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = mutate(d, X = ____))) - mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = d))
# ...
TipReveal solution 
d <- worlds |> filter(world == "D")
fit_d <- lm(Y ~ X + Z, data = d)
tidy(fit_d)
# A tibble: 3 x 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)     3.95    0.227       17.4 2.07e- 53
2 X              -2.98    0.0450     -66.3 6.88e-249
3 Z               2.06    0.0990      20.8 1.71e- 69
mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = mutate(d, X = X + 1))) - mean(predict(fit_d, newdata = d))
[1] -2.98139

Question 5. The coefficient on X and the averaged difference are the same number, and both are near \(-3\). Which result says the coefficient estimates the effect, which says the averaged difference does, and what about world D made both work? What would go wrong in world B, where the confounder e_u is in the table but would not be observed in practice?

TipReveal answer

The coefficient: the partialling-out theorem (week 2) says the coefficient on X in the long regression is the slope of Y on what is left of X after Z; in world D what is left is e_x, which is independent of everything else in Y, so the population value is \(-3\) and the sample coefficient estimates it. The averaged difference: the adjustment theorem, \(\mathbb E[Y \mid do(X = x)] = \mathbb E_Z[\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x, Z]]\), with the regression as the estimate of the inside. The two numbers coincide exactly because the fitted model is linear in X, so every unit’s difference is the coefficient. Both work because Z holds the only common cause of X and Y, is not a consequence of X, and the noises are independent. In world B the common cause is U, which you would not have: regress Y on X alone and you get the slope of about \(2\) from step 1, while the effect is \(0\). With e_u in the regression the coefficient on X is about \(0\): the theorem working, on a variable you have only because you simulated the world.

Question 6. Redraw the noise in intervene() (replace e_y by rnorm(n())) and look at Y_do - Y unit by unit in world A. What changes, and what does not? Which version is the counterfactual for a unit, and which is a new draw from the intervened world?

TipReveal answer

With the same noise every unit’s change is exactly \(2\) in world A; with fresh noise the unit-level differences scatter (variance \(2\)) while the average stays about \(2\). The first is the unit’s counterfactual: what would have happened to this unit. The second is a draw from the distribution after the intervention. Both have the same average effect; only the first answers “what if” for an individual, and in real data it is never observed, which is one reason causal inference is hard.

Optional, can be done at home: another dataset

Attrition (modeldata::attrition; fictional, made up by IBM data scientists, used only as an exercise): whether an employee leaves, with a threshold-and-costs story (a missed leaver costs a replacement, a false alarm costs a conversation). Leavers are 16 percent, so the accuracy-against-cost point is sharper: at threshold \(\tfrac12\) almost nobody is predicted to leave.

library(modeldata)
data(attrition)
att <- attrition |> mutate(left = as.numeric(Attrition == "Yes"))
fit_att <- glm(left ~ OverTime + MonthlyIncome + Age + JobSatisfaction, family = binomial, data = att)
# then steps 3, 4 and 5 with p = fitted(fit_att), costs 10 (a missed leaver) and 1 (a false alarm)
